To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
iron uptake and storage are region specific and age specific, and that the mechanisms for maintaining brain iron homeostasis are complex.

(1) the expression of proteins responsible to regulate iron uptake is region and age specific, (2) these proteins are expressed at a higher level in the brain of iron-deficient animals than in the brain of normal animals, (3) these proteins are also upregulated in response to iron excess in the diet, and (4) these proteins are differentially regulated in the brain in response to iron deficiency and excess.
the brain has the ability to regulate iron uptake by regulating the expression of iron management proteins in a region-specific manner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the brain maintains iron homeostasis and how this process may be disrupted in disease states.

the regulation of iron uptake and storage by the brain and the role of iron and iron management proteins (e.g., transferrin, transferrin receptor, and ferritin) in normal brain development, aging, and disease.

the mechanisms of iron acquisition by the brain, the mechanisms of iron storage in the brain, and the mechanisms that maintain iron homeostasis within specific regions of the brain and in specific cell types.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain is capable of maintaining a steady-state level of iron in the CNS by regulating the rate of iron uptake, the rate of iron utilization, and the rate of iron loss.
the brain is a highly regulated and compartmentalized organ with respect to its iron content and iron management proteins, and that this regulation is age and cell type specific.

iron homeostasis and its management in the brain is a complex and dynamic process that requires the coordinated expression of multiple proteins and that the expression patterns of these proteins are region specific and age dependent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain has a remarkable ability to regulate the uptake and distribution of iron to maintain iron homeostasis.
the brain is capable of storing a large amount of iron and that this storage is tightly regulated by a complex set of iron homeostasis proteins that are region and cell specific.
the brain, in its attempt to maintain homeostasis, is able to regulate iron acquisition and iron utilization in a region-specific manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
iron homeostasis is regulated in a regional and cell-specific manner, and that iron deficiency is more prevalent than iron excess in the CNS.
the brain is a dynamic iron-acquiring organ and is able to maintain iron homeostasis by regionally and cell type-specific expression of iron management proteins.
the brain is a dynamic system in which the expression of proteins responsible in maintaining iron homeostatic balance is regionally and developmentally specific.
